q: A patient 6 years after heart transplant becomes bradycardic (HR 40) under anaesthesia for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which drug is most likely to work?
why: The transplanted heart is denervated, so atropine and glycopyrronium have no vagolytic effect. Direct-acting drugs such as isoprenaline (or adrenaline, or pacing) work.

q: Why is the resting heart rate of a heart transplant recipient typically 90–110/min?
o: Loss of vagal tone to the donor sinus node
why: With no autonomic innervation the donor SA node runs at its intrinsic rate with no vagal brake. There is also no reflex tachycardia to laryngoscopy, fluid shifts or low BP.

q: A heart transplant recipient becomes hypotensive and needs adrenaline. How should it be dosed?
o: Larger doses, because receptors are downregulated
Smaller doses (e.g. 0.5 mcg increments), because receptors are upregulated
why: Receptor upregulation makes adrenaline and isoprenaline more potent, so start low. Indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine have unpredictable effects.

q: Why might cardiac allograft vasculopathy present without chest pain?
o: The denervated heart cannot signal ischaemic pain
Ischaemia does not occur in a transplanted heart
why: The myocardium is denervated, so ischaemia can be “silent”. Consider a cardiac catheter if vasculopathy is suspected.

q: Which analgesic should be avoided after surgery in a heart transplant patient taking ciclosporin?
why: NSAIDs add to the renal toxicity of calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus). Ciclosporin also causes hypertension and gingival hypertrophy, which can affect laryngoscopy.

q: A heart transplant recipient is planning pregnancy. Which immunosuppressant should be avoided?
why: Mycophenolate carries risks of miscarriage and congenital defects and is stopped before conception. Care is in a tertiary centre with immunosuppression continued.

q: After implantation of a donor heart, which is the commonest cause of difficult separation from bypass?
o: Right ventricular failure from raised PVR
why: The donor RV is not adapted to the recipient’s often raised PVR. Avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis, and use milrinone, adrenaline and inhaled nitric oxide.

q: A patient with a continuous-flow LVAD is under GA. NIBP and pulse oximetry readings are unreliable. Which monitoring is most useful?
why: Continuous flow means no palpable pulse on some devices, so NIBP and SpO2 can fail. Readings are independent of HR and EtCO2; TOE is the most useful, with invasive arterial monitoring.

q: An LVAD patient becomes hypotensive after induction and the console shows low flows. What is the most likely cause and treatment?
o: Device failure; switch the pump off
why: LVADs are preload-dependent, RV-dependent and afterload-sensitive. Vasodilatation at induction drops filling; restore preload and SVR, and call the LVAD team.

q: What is the mechanism of action of levosimendan?
o: Sensitising troponin C to calcium and opening ATP-sensitive K+ channels
why: Levosimendan is a calcium sensitiser and opens K-ATP channels (vasodilatation, reduced preload and afterload, better coronary perfusion). Milrinone and enoximone are PDE-III inhibitors; dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist.
